title: Hawkins v. McGee
caseType: Civil — breach of contract (appeal on damages)
questionPresented: What is the proper measure of damages when a surgeon guarantees a result and fails to deliver it?
facts: Plaintiff, a boy with a scarred hand from an electrical burn, underwent skin-graft surgery by defendant surgeon. Before the operation defendant told plaintiff's father: 'I will guarantee to make the hand a hundred per cent perfect hand.' The graft, taken from plaintiff's chest, left the hand hairy and in worse condition than before.
proceduralHistory: Jury returned verdict for plaintiff. Trial court set aside the verdict as excessive and instructed on damages as pain and suffering plus worsening of the hand. Plaintiff appeals.
plaintiffArguments: The guarantee was a contractual promise; damages should be the difference between the value of a perfect hand as promised and the hand as it is, like any warranty case.
defendantArguments: The statement was mere reassurance, not a contract; even if so, damages should be limited to pain and suffering and any worsening caused by the operation.
actualOutcome: New trial ordered; damages measured as difference between value of hand as promised and hand as delivered (expectation measure). Judgment for plaintiff on the measure of damages.

title: Palsgraf v. Long Island Railroad Co.
questionPresented: Does a railroad owe a duty of care to a bystander injured by an unforeseeable chain of events set off by its employees' negligence toward a different passenger?
facts: A passenger carrying a small package wrapped in newspaper ran to board a moving train. Two railroad guards helped him aboard; the package fell onto the rails and exploded — it contained fireworks, which nothing about its appearance revealed. The shock of the explosion knocked over scales at the far end of the platform, which struck and injured plaintiff, who was standing many feet away.
proceduralHistory: Jury verdict for plaintiff affirmed by Appellate Division. Defendant appeals.
plaintiffArguments: The guards were negligent in helping a passenger board a moving train; that negligence caused injury; defendant is liable for all consequences of its negligence.
defendantArguments: No duty was owed to plaintiff; any negligence was toward the boarding passenger only. Injury to plaintiff was unforeseeable; negligence is relational and there was no wrong done to her.
applicableLaw: Common-law negligence: duty, breach, causation, damages.
actualOutcome: Reversed; complaint dismissed. Judgment for defendant — no duty owed to plaintiff because harm to her was unforeseeable.

title: Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.
questionPresented: Did a newspaper advertisement promising £100 to anyone who used the product as directed and still caught influenza constitute a binding offer?
facts: Defendant advertised that it would pay £100 to any person who contracted influenza after using its smoke ball three times daily for two weeks, and stated £1000 was deposited with a bank 'shewing our sincerity in the matter.' Plaintiff bought a ball, used it as directed, and caught influenza.
proceduralHistory: Trial judge found for plaintiff. Defendant appeals.
plaintiffArguments: The advertisement was an offer to the world accepted by performance; the bank deposit shows intent to be bound; consideration was the inconvenience of use and benefit of increased sales.
defendantArguments: The advertisement was mere puff; there was no notification of acceptance, no consideration, and the terms were too vague to be a contract; it was a wager.
applicableLaw: English common law of contract: offer, acceptance, consideration, intention to create legal relations.
actualOutcome: Appeal dismissed; judgment for plaintiff. The advertisement was a binding unilateral offer accepted by performance.

title: Hadley v. Baxendale
questionPresented: Is a carrier liable for lost profits caused by delayed delivery when it was not told the delay would halt the customer's mill?
facts: Plaintiffs' mill stopped when a crankshaft broke. They engaged defendant carrier to deliver the broken shaft to the manufacturer as a pattern for a new one. Delivery was delayed by defendant's neglect, and the mill remained idle for several extra days. Plaintiffs sought lost profits for the idle period. The carrier's clerk was told only that the article was a broken shaft of a mill and that plaintiffs were the millers.
proceduralHistory: Jury awarded lost profits. Defendant moved for new trial on the ground of misdirection.
plaintiffArguments: Delay directly caused the mill to stand idle; lost profits are the natural result of the breach.
defendantArguments: Defendant had no notice that the mill would be stopped pending delivery; most millers keep a spare shaft; lost profits were not within the contemplation of the parties.
applicableLaw: Common-law contract damages; foreseeability / contemplation of the parties.
actualOutcome: New trial ordered; lost profits not recoverable because the special circumstances were not communicated to the carrier. Ruling for defendant on the damages question.

title: Rivera v. Northgate Properties LLC
questionPresented: Did the landlord unlawfully withhold the tenant's security deposit and act in bad faith?
facts: Tenant leased an apartment for 3 years at $2,400/month with a $4,800 deposit. On move-out, the landlord retained the entire deposit, citing carpet replacement ($3,100), repainting ($1,200), and cleaning ($500). Move-in inspection photos show the carpet was already 6 years old and showed wear. The landlord did not provide an itemized statement until 38 days after move-out, and provided no receipts.
evidence: Move-in and move-out photos; lease; landlord's itemized statement dated 38 days after move-out; carpet vendor invoice dated 2 years before tenancy showing original install; tenant's testimony that walls had only minor nail holes.
plaintiffArguments: Carpet had exceeded its useful life so replacement cannot be charged to the tenant; painting after a 3-year tenancy is normal wear and tear; the statement was late and unsupported by receipts; the retention was in bad faith warranting statutory penalties.
defendantArguments: Carpet had stains beyond normal wear; walls had scuffs requiring full repaint; the delay in the statement was a clerical oversight, not bad faith.
applicableLaw: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5: deposit may be used only for unpaid rent, cleaning, and repair of damage beyond ordinary wear and tear; itemized statement with receipts must be provided within 21 days; bad-faith retention subjects landlord to statutory damages up to twice the deposit.
actualOutcome: Judgment for tenant for return of full deposit plus statutory bad-faith penalty.
